This is usually done by grinding a small portion of the fossil into a fine powder and then using chemicals to break down the cells and release the DNA. The DNA is then purified and concentrated using various methods, such as silica-based columns or magnetic beads.

2. Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR): PCR is a technique used to amplify specific regions of the DNA, making it easier to analyze. Scientists design short pieces of DNA called primers that are complementary to the target DNA sequence. The PCR process involves multiple cycles of heating and cooling, which cause the DNA to separate, bind to the primers, and then be copied by a heat-resistant enzyme called Taq polymerase. 3. Sequencing: Once the DNA has been extracted and amplified, it can be sequenced to determine the order of the nucleotides (A, T, C, and G) that make up the genetic code. These methods allow scientists to read the DNA sequences and compare them to those of other species.
